extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of natural philosophy / readers of classical scientific treatises
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a Latin natural-philosophical treatise ( De Elementis ), discussing water, seas, rivers, springs, tides, and related natural phenomena; intended for study/translation and analysis of historical theories of hydrology and elemental theory. Contains classifications, causal claims, and empirical signs/examples used by the author to explain and diagnose water-related phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite ordering of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three elements: air (the lightest and largest), earth (next in magnitude), and water (intermediate in magnitude and positioned between air and earth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses this ordering to explain why land is mostly surface-occupied (for generation and habitation) and why water is of limited quantity relative to earth. Consequences drawn include distribution of elements in layers (air above, water in middle, earth below) and implications for habitation, generation of animals/plants, and the impossibility of water occupying the same magnitude as earth without submerging life. Examples/discussion around how this ordering affects inundations and the relative positions of cold/heat near poles and equator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of water bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct kinds of water-bodies are identified and named: mare (sea, in a hollow communicating broadly), lacus (fresh lake), palus (marsh, if not moving), stagnum (stagnant when abundant), fluvius/fluens (river/stream when flowing), fons (spring), torrens (torrent from rains/snow), rivulus (small rivulet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives linguistic/functional distinctions and examples (e.g., particular named marshes and seas). This classification is used as a basis for further causal explanations (e.g., why certain water types become saline, form lakes, or dry up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of rivers and springs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rivers and springs may originate from several causes: from the sea (rare/controversial), from rains and snows gathering, from subterranean sources where water ascends after descending from higher places, and from mountain melt/underground conduits; many springs derive from water collected and transmitted from higher terrains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues against the sea being the source of high springs: water does not rise from sea to mountain height; rather, subterranean motion and mountain-fed descent-ascent account for springs. Uses examples (Tanais, Tigris, Indus, Nile) and observations about well salinity and proximity to sea as evidence. Guidance includes diagnostic signs: proximity to sea reducing salinity in wells, admixture of fresh water, and the impossibility, by simple ratio, of sea water ascending to mountain tops without intermediate processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and mechanics of inundations (floods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Floods arise where water collects in cavities or low places, where inflows (rivers, rains, melting snow) accumulate faster than outflow, or where seasonal increases (e.g., Nile inundations) occur; geography (sloping toward the south, low places) and solar heating patterns influence inundation occurrence and extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations include how shallow basins fill, how accumulation over months can lead to large inundations, and why some regions are repeatedly flooded (reference to Plato/Timæus and Herodotus on Nile periodicity). The author discusses why many floods would be rare if water were uniformly abundant, and how local topography and climate (solar heat, seasonal rains) modulate floods. Examples: Nile's rising and falling, local marsh management practices (irrigation/dewatering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of sea salinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Salinity of the sea (and of some lakes) is attributed to factors like persistent solar heat, water that does not run off (allowing putrefaction/concentration), and continuity/accumulation of briny matter: evaporation concentrates salts and leaves the sea 'salty'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists three conditions sufficient to maintain salinity: solar heat, lack of outflow so rainwater and other inputs concentrate and putrefy, and continuity/connection of waters. He contrasts seas that are salt with inland sweet lakes and marshes, and discusses regional examples (Mediterranean, Dead Sea, etc.). The text uses empirical indicators (e.g., certain lakes being salt despite apparent separation) and appeals to ancient authorities (Ptolemy, Pliny) while noting differences of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lunar (and stellar) influence on tides
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement of seas (tides and ebb/flow) is linked to the motion of the moon and stars; tidal magnitude varies with lunar phase (greatest at full and new moons, least at quadratures) and follows a cycle tied to lunar position relative to the horizon (approx. a daily-return rhythm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explains observed periodicities (greater motion at certain lunar positions, smaller at others) and gives observational notes (e.g., Mediterranean tides, local differences near equinoxes and tropics). The text also discusses how the moon's position (and its daily return) explains why ships appear to move particular distances daily. Uses astronomical reasoning developed in earlier chapters as the basis for tidal causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs for freshwater origin versus marine origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that a spring or well derives from the sea include salinity gradients with distance (wells nearer the sea often more saline), admixture of other fresh waters reducing salinity, and the relative depth/length of subterranean conduits; conversely, fresh springs often show absence of salinity and have particular organoleptic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author offers heuristics: measure salinity relative to distance from the sea, consider admixture of inland waters, check for purgation by earth/filtration, and test taste/odour. He cautions that proximity alone is not conclusive and discusses how sea-derived brine could be diluted or purified by passage through earth and sediments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of potable and 'good' waters
rubrics_metrics.description: Good/healthful water is described as colorless, odorless, pleasant in taste, clear, and not liable to remain in the belly (i.e., not causing digestion problems); specific rivers are cited as exemplars (e.g., Eulzi, Choaspes, Tyber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses organoleptic tests (look, smell, taste) and practical effects (does the water preserve health?) to judge water quality. Regional examples illustrate how soil and nearby geology (bitumen, metals, clays) affect water quality. The author notes historical reverence for certain streams and the practical choices of rulers who favored particular waters for drinking or campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of hot springs and subterranean heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Hot springs and subterranean flames are ascribed to combustible materials underground (bitumen, sulphur), the presence of 'respiration' (air/oxygen), and motion; heat is not necessarily perpetual and eruptions can be intermittent, affected by winds and changes in subterranean conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives a threefold account of conditions needed for subterranean fire: combustible matter (e.g., bitumen), material that respires or provides oxidation, and motion that facilitates ignition; examples include local hot springs and fumaroles. He argues for non-permanence of subterranean fire, explains intermittent flaring after winds, and describes how bituminous deposits and drying favour ignition. There are cautions about assuming celestial fire alone explains hot springs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal and daily rhythms of river flow
rubrics_metrics.description: River discharge varies seasonally and diurnally: rivers often swell in the morning and in seasons associated with melting snows and rains (spring/early summer), while they diminish in autumn and are generally lower in winter; local climatic patterns can invert these trends in some places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations include melting of snow in mountains, nocturnal condensation/precipitation increasing morning flows, and seasonal patterns recorded for specific rivers (e.g., Nile's cycle as reported by Herodotus and Strabo). The author notes regional exceptions depending on local climate and basin characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of geology/soil in water properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the surrounding earth (bituminous strata, clays, salines, metals) imparts properties to water: oily or odorous waters arise near bitumen, colored waters come from clays, and mineral-rich waters reflect contact with metallic or bituminous ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites regional examples where soils produce characteristic waters (bituminous springs producing oil, clay producing certain tints). It uses such signs both diagnostically (to infer the underlying ground) and prescriptively (to recommend or avoid certain waters for health or utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightness/heaviness and stratification of waters
rubrics_metrics.description: Waters differ in specific gravity: lighter waters float above heavier waters; heavy parts sink while lighter parts remain on top (affecting flotation of objects and relative positions of mixtures such as oils on water).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is applied to explain why some waters are more buoyant, why oils and foams behave as they do, and to account for variation within rivers, springs, and seas. The author refers to Aristotle's broader doctrine about lightness/levity and applies it to aquatic phenomena (e.g., foamy regions produce lithification, lighter parts ascend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for lake formation and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Lakes arise where many waters flow into an ample cavity; permanence depends on the balance of inflow versus outflow and on the basin's ability to retain water against evaporation and percolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains that when inflow fills a hollow, a lake forms; permanence (or conversion into marsh or drying) depends on inflow rates, subterranean drainage, evaporation, and climatic heating. Examples and counterexamples are discussed (certain lakes becoming part of the continent or shrinking due to sedimentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation of stones and petrifaction in aquatic contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Stony material and petrifaction can arise in water through accumulation of foam, sand and salts, and through processes where organic matter (e.g., wood, bark) becomes stone-like when encrusted by mineral deposits in certain marine or riverine conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author provides reports of trees, bark, and nests petrified in seas or rivers, attributing formation to repeated deposition of mineral-laden foam and sand. This is used to explain occurrences of lapides generated in rivers and seas and relates to observed local phenomena near coasts and torrents.
